# Nebius raises GPU prices 20% as supply tightens

The neocloud expansion, from Sharon AI's Australian buildout to FluidStack's $1.5 billion round, shows how GPU capacity providers finance and site AI compute.

By Arjun Mehta, Infrastructure correspondent Published Sep 16, 2026, 07:00 UTC 2 min read

Multiple NVIDIA H100 data-center GPUs, the hardware whose cloud rental prices Nebius is raising. Photograph: 极客湾Geekerwan/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 3.0)

By September 16, 2026, the AI neocloud expansion had reached a pricing inflection. BigGo Finance reported that Nebius said it will raise GPU cloud prices by an average of 20 percent from October 1, covering H100, H200, B200 and B300 chips, with B300 rising from $7.85 to $9.50 per GPU-hour. The announcement pushed Nebius shares up nearly 7 percent in after-hours trading.

That increase followed a financing and siting rush that enterprises watched closely. On August 4, 2026, Sharon AI signed a five-year, $373 million contract with a global AI platform customer for AI cloud services, according to tech-insider.org. The first deployment uses 2,048 Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs hosted in NEXTDC data centres in Melbourne and Sydney.

On August 7, 2026, Dentons published an analysis of how such projects get funded. AI-optimized facilities often separate the building shell from the GPU hardware in their capital stacks. Lenders fund the shell, while the chips may be supported through equipment finance, loans secured by the GPUs, or financing from the vendor. The main structural safeguard is a hyperscaler backstop, which turns short-dated neocloud revenue into investment-grade streams. Dentons cited Microsoft's commitment to CoreWeave, which accounted for 62 percent of CoreWeave revenue in 2024 and 67 percent in 2025. Dentons also warned that neocloud counterparties are sub-investment-grade and depend on Nvidia supply.

Data Centre Magazine's August 12 top-10 list noted that Crusoe had raised more than $13 billion in institutional capital and held a multi-gigawatt clean energy pipeline, while CoreWeave had priority access to Nvidia's latest accelerators and long-term deals with Meta and Microsoft.

On August 19, 2026, Nebius priced $5.0 billion in convertible notes, according to a comparison published by MarkTechPost on August 23. The same report said CoreWeave's second-quarter revenue reached $2.575 billion, up 112 percent year over year, while Nebius reported $582.3 million, up 454 percent, with $3.0 billion of AI cloud annualised recurring revenue.

Crusoe reported 4.9 gigawatts of contracted AI infrastructure across five US campuses, with a development pipeline above 40 gigawatts. Sharon AI's total contracted capacity was 132 megawatts, 102 megawatts of which was already under contract, according to tech-insider.org. The same source said Sharon AI planned more than 55,000 GPUs by mid-2027, including a 72-megawatt Nvidia collaboration targeting up to 40,000 GB300 chips.

On September 5, 2026, Tech Times reported that FluidStack closed a $1.5 billion round led by Jane Street at an $18 billion valuation. FluidStack holds no chips itself; it builds modular data centres and runs chip-agnostic clusters for customers such as Anthropic, with Google backstopping billions of dollars in lease obligations at former crypto mining sites.

The latest price signal matters for enterprises purchasing AI compute. Nebius's increase is its second since May, and it follows auction tests where customers paid 15 to 20 percent above the previous maximum listed price for scarce Blackwell capacity. Nebius also said demand visibility now extends beyond 24 months. tech-insider.org reported that committed-contract discounts can reach 60 percent off list price but require multi-year commitments, and recommended hybrid architectures that keep general workloads on hyperscalers while routing GPU-intensive jobs to neoclouds.

Arjun Mehta covers data centres, AI infrastructure and networks for Five Nines. He writes from company announcements, filings and published reporting.

# Nebius to Raise GPU Cloud Pricing Across H100, H200, B200 and B300 Starting Oct. 1

Nebius will raise on-demand GPU cloud pricing across H100, H200, B200 and B300 starting October 1, as it scales capacity and secures financing tied to deployed GPUs.

Published Sep 17, 2026 · 4:44 PM ET · 4 min read

## Nebius to Raise GPU Cloud Pricing Across H100, H200, B200 and B300 Starting Oct. 1— Sep 17, 2026

The AI infrastructure provider is lifting on-demand compute rates as it scales global capacity and secures fresh financing tied to deployed GPUs — coming off a quarter in which AI Cloud revenue surged 514%.

In this article

1. What's changing
2. Why Nebius is raising prices
3. The Q2 backdrop
4. What to watch
5. The takeaway
6. Frequently Asked Questions

Nebius Group (NASDAQ: NBIS) is planning to raise prices on several of its on-demand GPU, CPU, and memory services starting October 1, according to a customer pricing notice reviewed by MarketCatalyst. The adjustments touch the company's most sought-after compute tiers — NVIDIA's H100, H200, B200, and B300 chips — and follow a strong second quarter shaped by rising AI Cloud demand.

For a company whose appeal to customers has largely rested on offering discounted capacity relative to the hyperscalers, a broad rate increase is worth noting. It may suggest that Nebius feels demand for its infrastructure is steady enough to comfortably absorb higher prices, without meaningfully affecting customer retention.

## What's Changing

The notice lists new per-GPU-hour rates across four NVIDIA chip families, plus adjustments to underlying CPU and memory pricing:

| Hardware | New Rate | Previous Rate | Region(s) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA H100 | $4.50 / GPU-hr | $3.85 / GPU-hr | eu-north1 |
| NVIDIA H200 | $5.40 / GPU-hr | $4.50 / GPU-hr | Listed European & U.S. regions |
| NVIDIA B200 | $8.50 / GPU-hr | $7.15 / GPU-hr | us-central1, me-west1 |
| NVIDIA B300 | $9.50 / GPU-hr | $7.85 / GPU-hr | uk-south1, eu-west2, us-north1 |

The increases range from roughly 15% for the H100 and H200 to about 21% for the B300, which sees the largest adjustment of the four. AMD EPYC Genoa CPU and memory rates are also moving slightly higher as part of the same notice, while Intel Ice Lake CPU pricing remains unchanged.

The bottom line

Every chip seeing a price increase is a current-generation or near-current NVIDIA accelerator used for AI training and inference, rather than older, lower-demand hardware. This pattern is consistent with a company adjusting prices where capacity is tightest, rather than where it may be trying to move idle inventory.

## Why Nebius Is Raising Prices

Nebius describes the changes as part of scaling its global AI infrastructure and securing additional financing tied to deployed GPUs — language that points toward asset-backed financing structures, where lenders extend capital against contracted or installed hardware. In that context, pricing is likely about more than margin alone: higher effective revenue per GPU can also help support the economics that lenders and customers are underwriting against.

This also appears consistent with what Nebius has shared with investors more broadly. On its Q2 earnings call, management noted that the company has repeatedly sold out of available capacity as new supply comes online, and pointed to a capacity auction that cleared at a record price, roughly 15% above previous highs for Blackwell-generation chips. Taken together, these details suggest demand has been outpacing supply, and this notice may reflect Nebius adjusting its list prices accordingly.

## The Q2 Backdrop

The price increases follow a second quarter in which Nebius's core cloud business scaled sharply:

+514% AI Cloud revenue growth, YoY

$236.2M Adjusted EBITDA (from a $21M loss)

$582.3M Group revenue, +454% YoY

$3.0B Annualized run-rate revenue, June-end

Nebius has reaffirmed 2026 guidance calling for $3–$3.4 billion in group revenue, a roughly 40% adjusted EBITDA margin, and $20–$25 billion in capital expenditures as it continues building out data center capacity globally. Higher on-demand rates may offer the company an additional path toward those targets, without necessarily requiring capacity growth to move faster than planned.

## What to Watch

Worth remembering

Price increases on scarce, high-demand hardware often reflect pricing power in the moment, though they're also a factor customers tend to watch closely over time. Should rivals with newer or more affordably priced capacity emerge, some price-sensitive workloads could gradually shift elsewhere. For now, sold-out capacity and strong auction pricing suggest Nebius isn't yet facing that kind of pressure.

The rate changes are set to take effect October 1 across the regions listed above. Customers with existing reserved or contracted capacity commitments are typically governed by separate contract terms rather than these on-demand list prices, though the notice offers a useful signal on the broader direction of AI compute costs as capacity remains tight across the industry.

## The Takeaway

- This appears to be a pricing-power story rather than a distress signal. Every hardware tier seeing an increase is among Nebius's newest, most in-demand GPU capacity — the kind of asset that tends to see higher prices when demand outpaces supply.
- It's broadly consistent with the Q2 narrative. Sold-out capacity, strong auction clearing prices, and a 514% AI Cloud revenue surge all point in a similar direction: customer demand currently appears to be outpacing what Nebius can immediately supply.
- Financing and pricing seem increasingly connected. Tying new financing to deployed GPUs may make the economics of each GPU — including what it can be rented for — more directly relevant to Nebius's capital structure, and not just its income statement.
